C0.quote: explores the effects of the straight-ticket voting option (STVO)
C0.note: Borderline: a probabilistic-voting model of how a ballot-design feature (STVO) shapes outcomes of elections. Treated as eligible because the object is a voting procedure and its effects.

C1.quote: We solve the game by backward induction.
C1.note: Subgame-perfect analysis of a party-voter game with comparative statics (Propositions 1-3). The motivating data in Fig. 1 is descriptive and not a main result.

C2.1.value: ballot (race-by-race votes or a straight-ticket vote)
C2.1.quote: allows voters to select one party for all partisan elections

C2.2.quote: he selects the candidate that maximises uik (j)
C2.2.note: Each voter casts a vote for one of two parties' candidates in each race, or a single straight-party vote. This is a choice among two alternatives, not a ranking, approval set, or the other listed formats.

C2.3.quote: Voters’ utility from electing a candidate has three components
C2.3.note: Voters hold bliss points, a partisanship status, and utilities.

C2.4.quote: if the voter does not use the STVO and goes through the ballot
C2.4.note: Utility and bliss points are held attitudes with separate notation. The vote is a separate object: a voter who uses STVO votes the party line even where race-level utility would favour another candidate.

C3.1.quote: although they would have voted positionally had the option not been made available
C3.1.note: Borderline. Voters choosing STVO submit a straight ticket that may differ from their race-by-race utility-maximising choice, but this is not strategic misreporting; it is a cost-driven choice of ballot. Coded ALL because the voter-choice analysis is the core of every result.

C4.1.note: The input format is not RANK, WEAK, APPR, DICH or PAIR.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.quote: deduce its effects on three outcomes: candidates’ platforms
C5.1.note: Results concern platforms, vote shares and the expected position of the winner. No welfare, efficiency, representation or distortion criterion is evaluated.

VOT.quote_behav: He makes his decision by comparing the cost
VOT.note: Voters decide whether to use STVO by comparing cost with expected benefit. They observe candidate positions and party labels, and the quality shock only when going through the ballot. Their knowledge of other voters' attitudes or inputs is not specified.

CAN.quote_behav: The party derives utility from the vote share
CAN.quote_info: its distribution is common knowledge so our model contains no aggregate uncertainty
CAN.note: Parties act as proponents who select candidates. They know the distributions of voter positions and partisanship, but not individual realisations.

DES.note: STVO availability is an exogenous parameter (mu).

C7.1.quote: Our model of an election with STVO is a game
C7.1.note: Both voters and parties are strategic.

C8.1.quote: We solve the game by backward induction.

C9.1.note: Claims concern real institutions and ballot design.

C9.2.quote: Voters’ utility from electing a candidate has three components
C9.2.note: The claims rest on the probabilistic voting model, the party objective, and free candidate choice. The paper states all of these. No voter-welfare claim is made, so no input-attitude link is needed.
